projects.title: Three degrees of play.
projects.summary: A tabletop game with a three-degree-of-freedom opponent: X, Y, and rotation, moving through randomized patterns.
projects.problem: Build a mechanism with at least 2.5 degrees of freedom. Our team turned the assignment into a tabletop game: a human player competes against a moving mechanism to score through goal cutouts.
projects.decisions: We chose three degrees of freedom: translation in X and Y, plus rotation. Randomized motion makes the opponent less predictable. The player can flick the puck, as in carrom, or use a mallet, as in air hockey.
projects.development: Designed the mechanism and its components in CAD, then built a working game. The video shows the completed game. The interactive assembly combines our supplied component geometry with a reconstruction of the surrounding hardware.
projects.results: Completed a playable prototype with translation and rotation. The demonstration documents the game in use.
projects.technical:
Motion: X translation, Y translation, and rotation. The complete presentation assembly combines supplied STL meshes with reference geometry reconstructed from the video. Table, rails, belts, pulleys, fasteners, motor housings and electronics are simplified. Dimensions and placements are approximate; this is not fabrication-ready or mechanically validated CAD. Individual supplied parts remain available in the component menu.

Documentation still to add: first linear-stage revision, confirmed manufacturing methods/materials, individual team contributions and quantitative test results. MATLAB files are supplied as project source for review; their settings are specific to the class hardware.

gallery.caption: The completed ENG ME 360 game in play.

sections.title: Brief & function
sections.body: For ENG ME 360, our team had to build a system with at least 2.5 degrees of freedom. We made a tabletop game with a mechanism that translates in X and Y and rotates a mallet. A player flicks the puck or uses a handheld mallet to score through goal openings while the mechanism follows randomized motion.

sections.title: Linear stage & gantry
sections.body: The two linear axes position the mallet over the playing surface. The source code synchronizes two bridge motors through the X and E1 drivers, then moves the transverse carriage with the Y driver. Keeping the bridge square matters because the two sides must travel together. The available carriage, slider-holder and motor-mount CAD can be inspected individually in the viewer.

sections.title: Final assembly
sections.body: The built system combines the playing surface, longitudinal rails, transverse gantry, carriage, rotary drive and mallet. The video shows the working hardware. The complete 3D assembly is a presentation reconstruction using our supplied STL geometry; surrounding hardware and placement are approximate.

sections.title: Construction & manufacturing
sections.body: Custom brackets and holders connect the linear guides, motors and mallet to an extrusion-based frame. The supplied SolidWorks parts and STL exports document the component geometry. Exact material, fabrication process and assembly tolerances have not yet been documented here.

sections.title: Control software
sections.body: The final MATLAB loop sends G-code over a serial connection. It positions the bridge, queues alternating randomized Y destinations, returns the carriage to its midpoint and returns the bridge to its start. The rotary motor stays powered during motion. The code waits for controller acknowledgements and uses M400 when it needs motion to finish. Its coordinate zero is set manually; it does not perform a homing search. The rotary channel is PWM power control, not closed-loop angular positioning: two positioned linear axes plus powered rotation satisfy the 2.5+ DOF brief.

sections.title: Demonstration & outcome
sections.body: The completed game is shown in play in the video above. The demonstration establishes a working prototype; repeatability, positioning error and game performance have not been measured in this case study.

projects.title: Class plotter exercise.
projects.summary: A two-axis pen plotter: turning coordinated linear motion into a drawing on paper.
projects.tools: Linear stages / lead screws / pen carriage

sections.title: Exercise & function
sections.body: The class exercise uses a pen mounted on a moving carriage to turn two-axis positioning into a drawing. Coordinating travel along the two linear axes moves the pen across the paper.

sections.title: Mechanism & assembly
sections.body: The demonstration shows an extrusion-supported frame, threaded drive elements, motors and a pen carriage. One stage carries the transverse structure; the second positions the pen along it. Together they generate motion in the drawing plane.

sections.title: Example control approach
sections.body: A reconstructed MATLAB example shows how a drawing can be represented by XY waypoints, interpolated into small movements and animated as a pen trace. It closes a rectangular path and calculates idealized travel time at a constant feed rate. The dimensions and timing are illustrative. This example was created after the class exercise; it is not the source used in the demonstration and has not been tested on the original hardware.

sections.title: Construction
sections.body: The rig combines structural extrusion with custom supports and a pen holder. The video documents the assembled mechanism. The original component CAD, first-stage design revision and exact manufacturing methods for this exercise have not yet been supplied.

sections.title: Demonstration & outcome
sections.body: The video shows the pen drawing a geometric outline on paper. It records the exercise in operation; drawing accuracy, repeatability and speed have not been quantified here.

projects.technical: Supporting evidence: original class demonstration video. The downloadable MATLAB example is a later simulation-only reconstruction, not the original plotter-control code. It sends no hardware commands. Plotter-specific CAD, first linear-stage revision, manufacturing details and original classroom source remain to be added.
